Understanding the characteristics that make a good representation remains a topic of ongoing research. Disentanglement of independent generative processes has long been credited with producing high-quality representations. However, focusing solely on representations that adhere to the stringent requirements of most disentanglement metrics, may result in overlooking many high-quality representations, well suited for various downstream tasks. These metrics often demand that generative factors be encoded in distinct, single dimensions aligned with the canonical basis of the representation space. Motivated by these observations, we propose two novel metrics: Importance-Weighted Orthogonality (IWO) and Importance-Weighted Rank (IWR). These metrics evaluate the mutual orthogonality and rank of generative factor subspaces. Throughout extensive experiments on common downstream tasks, over several benchmark datasets and models, IWO and IWR consistently show stronger correlations with downstream task performance than traditional disentanglement metrics. Our findings suggest that representation quality is closer related to the orthogonality of independent generative processes rather than their disentanglement, offering a new direction for evaluating and improving unsupervised learning models.

papers.title: Learning through atypical phase transitions in overparameterized neural networks
papers.research_question: How does overparameterization affect the geometrical structure of minima in non-convex neural networks, and how does this relate to learning and generalization performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that overparameterized non-convex neural networks exhibit two phase transitions: the interpolation threshold and the Local Entropy transition, and that efficient learning algorithms sample from wide, atypical minima with good generalization, despite typical minima being sharp and numerous.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that atypical phase transitions driven by rare, wide minima are key to understanding learning in overparameterized non-convex networks.
papers.key_findings:
There are two phase transitions: the interpolation threshold (where solutions appear) and the Local Entropy transition (where wide minima appear).
Typical solutions are sharp and isolated, with poor generalization.
Atypical solutions are wide and dense, with good generalization, and are sampled by efficient algorithms.
The Local Entropy transition is the relevant one for learning.
Numerical experiments on various architectures confirm the theoretical predictions.
future_direction: Conduct in-depth numerical studies of large deep networks.
Corroborate results with rigorous bounds for more general data distributions.
Theoretical confirmation that dynamics of a broad class of algorithms is attracted to these structures.
papers.abstract: Current deep neural networks are highly overparameterized (up to billions of connection weights) and nonlinear. Yet they can fit data almost perfectly through variants of gradient descent algorithms and achieve unexpected levels of prediction accuracy without overfitting. These are formidable results that defy predictions of statistical learning and pose conceptual challenges for nonconvex optimization. In this paper, we use methods from statistical physics of disordered systems to analytically study the computational fallout of overparameterization in nonconvex binary neural network models, trained on data generated from a structurally simpler but "hidden" network. As the number of connection weights increases, we follow the changes of the geometrical structure of different minima of the error loss function and relate them to learning and generalization performance. A first transition happens at the so-called interpolation point, when solutions begin to exist (perfect fitting becomes possible). This transition reflects the properties of typical solutions, which however are in sharp minima and hard to sample. After a gap, a second transition occurs, with the discontinuous appearance of a different kind of "atypical" structures: wide regions of the weight space that are particularly solution dense and have good generalization properties. The two kinds of solutions coexist, with the typical ones being exponentially more numerous, but empirically we find that efficient algorithms sample the atypical, rare ones. This suggests that the atypical phase transition is the relevant one for learning. The results of numerical tests with realistic networks on observables suggested by the theory are consistent with this scenario.

papers.title: Decomposing Representation Space into Interpretable Subspaces with Unsupervised Learning
papers.research_question: Can we find interpretable subspaces in neural representations in an unsupervised way? To what extent are different aspects organized in separate subspaces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an unsupervised method (NDM) to decompose representation space into interpretable subspaces, showing that these subspaces align with known circuit variables and can serve as new basic units for circuit analysis.
papers.conclusion: Unsupervised decomposition of representation space into interpretable subspaces is possible, and these subspaces can serve as new basic units for circuit analysis, offering a new perspective on understanding model internals.
papers.key_findings:
NDM can find interpretable subspaces without supervision, as shown in toy models and real language models.
Subspaces found by NDM align with variables in known circuits in GPT-2, as evidenced by high Gini coefficients in subspace patching experiments.
The method scales to 2B models, finding separate subspaces for context and parametric knowledge routing.
Qualitative analysis shows that subspaces are consistent and interpretable across different inputs.
papers.limitation: The method can get stuck in local minima, leading to sub-optimal subspace partitions.
future_direction: hierarchical structure of subspaces
more flexible searching over dimension configurations
applying the method to larger models and more tasks
papers.abstract: Understanding internal representations of neural models is a core interest of mechanistic interpretability. Due to its large dimensionality, the representation space can encode various aspects about inputs. To what extent are different aspects organized and encoded in separate subspaces? Is it possible to find these ``natural'' subspaces in a purely unsupervised way? Somewhat surprisingly, we can indeed achieve this and find interpretable subspaces by a seemingly unrelated training objective. Our method, neighbor distance minimization (NDM), learns non-basis-aligned subspaces in an unsupervised manner. Qualitative analysis shows subspaces are interpretable in many cases, and encoded information in obtained subspaces tends to share the same abstract concept across different inputs, making such subspaces similar to ``variables'' used by the model. We also conduct quantitative experiments using known circuits in GPT-2; results show a strong connection between subspaces and circuit variables. We also provide evidence showing scalability to 2B models by finding separate subspaces mediating context and parametric knowledge routing. Viewed more broadly, our findings offer a new perspective on understanding model internals and building circuits.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability as Statistical Estimation: A Variance Analysis
papers.research_question: What is the stability of mechanistic interpretability methods, specifically circuit discovery, and how does variance in causal mediation analysis and its approximations affect the reliability of discovered circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that circuit discovery methods are highly unstable due to intrinsic variance in causal mediation analysis scores and amplification by approximation methods, advocating for more rigorous statistical practices in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Circuit discovery is not a stable process and requires statistical rigor, including reporting stability metrics and sensitivity analyses, to become a reliable scientific tool.
papers.key_findings:
Exact causal mediation analysis (CMA) scores exhibit high intrinsic variance across inputs, meaning the causal effect of a component is a volatile random variable.
Approximation methods like Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) amplify this variance, leading to low signal-to-noise ratios.
Circuit discovery pipelines are sensitive to data resampling, hyperparameters, and counterfactual definitions, resulting in structurally inconsistent circuits.
Larger models (e.g., Llama-3.2-1B) show higher variability in circuit discovery compared to smaller models (e.g., gpt2-small).
The instability of circuits is not mitigated by instruction tuning (comparing Llama-3.2-1B and its instruct variant).
papers.limitation:
Focus on the EAP family of methods, leaving out newer methods that may have different properties.
Exact CMA analysis was only done on gpt2-small for the IOI task due to computational constraints.
Limited to three classic MI tasks, which may not generalize to fuzzier reasoning tasks.
Stability metrics treat all edges equally, whereas weighted metrics might reveal a stable functional core.
future_direction: Probabilistic circuit discovery: characterizing a distribution over possible circuits.
Decomposing variance into estimator variance and intrinsic variance.
Stability-aware optimization: developing objectives that explicitly optimize for stability.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) aims to reverse-engineer model behaviors by identifying functional sub-networks. Yet, the scientific validity of these findings depends on their stability. In this work, we argue that circuit discovery is not a standalone task but a statistical estimation problem built upon causal mediation analysis (CMA). We uncover a fundamental instability at this base layer: exact, single-input CMA scores exhibit high intrinsic variance, implying that the causal effect of a component is a volatile random variable rather than a fixed property. We then demonstrate that circuit discovery pipelines inherit this variance and further amplify it. Fast approximation methods, such as Edge Attribution Patching and its successors, introduce additional estimation noise, while aggregating these noisy scores over datasets leads to fragile structural estimates. Consequently, small perturbations in input data or hyperparameters yield vastly different circuits. We systematically decompose these sources of variance and advocate for more rigorous MI practices, prioritizing statistical robustness and routine reporting of stability metrics.

papers.title: Towards scientific discovery with dictionary learning: Extracting biological concepts from microscopy foundation models
papers.research_question: Can dictionary learning extract meaningful high-level concepts from unsupervised vision foundation models trained on scientific data (cell microscopy images) where prior knowledge about concepts is limited?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ICFL, a novel sparse dictionary learning algorithm combined with PCA whitening, to successfully extract biologically meaningful concepts (e.g., cell types, genetic perturbations) from frozen representations of vision foundation models trained on cell microscopy images.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary learning, specifically ICFL with PCA whitening, is a powerful and promising approach for extracting interpretable biological concepts from microscopy foundation models, enabling new directions for scientific discovery via mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
ICFL combined with PCA whitening extracts sparse features that correlate with biological concepts such as cell types and genetic perturbations.
ICFL reduces the number of 'dead features' compared to TopK SAEs.
Linear probes on reconstructions from ICFL features preserve significant biological information, with accuracies comparable to probes on original representations.
ICFL features achieve selectivity scores comparable to handcrafted CellProfiler features for identifying genetic perturbations.
Token-level heatmaps from feature directions enable interpretation of subtle morphological changes, such as distinguishing perturbed from control-like cells.
future_direction: Assess whether peak selectivity of handcrafted features can be matched using deep learning-based approaches with fewer non-zero elements.
Future research on interpreting and validating concept directions found in large foundation models for microscopy image data.
papers.abstract: Sparse dictionary learning (DL) has emerged as a powerful approach to extract semantically meaningful concepts from the internals of large language models (LLMs) trained mainly in the text domain. In this work, we explore whether DL can extract meaningful concepts from less human-interpretable scientific data, such as vision foundation models trained on cell microscopy images, where limited prior knowledge exists about which high-level concepts should arise. We propose a novel combination of a sparse DL algorithm, Iterative Codebook Feature Learning (ICFL), with a PCA whitening pre-processing step derived from control data. Using this combined approach, we successfully retrieve biologically meaningful concepts, such as cell types and genetic perturbations. Moreover, we demonstrate how our method reveals subtle morphological changes arising from human-interpretable interventions, offering a promising new direction for scientific discovery via mechanistic interpretability in bioimaging.

papers.title: Towards Automated Circuit Discovery for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we automate the discovery of circuits in neural networks for mechanistic interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper systematizes the mechanistic interpretability workflow and introduces the ACDC algorithm to automate circuit discovery by using activation patching to find important connections in the computational graph.
papers.conclusion: ACDC is a step towards automating circuit discovery in mechanistic interpretability, showing promise on several tasks but with limitations that need to be addressed in future work.
papers.key_findings:
ACDC successfully rediscovers known circuits, such as the Greater-Than circuit in GPT-2 Small and the IOI circuit.
ACDC selects a sparse set of edges (e.g., 68 out of 32,000 in GPT-2 Small for IOI) that match manually found circuits.
ACDC performs competitively with gradient-based methods like Subnetwork Probing and Head Importance Score for Pruning.
ACDC is not robust in all settings, e.g., it fails on tracr tasks when using corrupted activations.
ACDC can miss negative components when optimizing for logit difference.
papers.limitation:
ACDC can fail in some settings, such as on tracr tasks when using corrupted activations.
ACDC may miss negative components when optimizing for logit difference.
The ground-truth circuits from previous work are not 100% reliable, limiting the evaluation.
future_direction: Automating the functional interpretation of model components.
Improving circuit discovery methods to handle more complex behaviors and models.
papers.abstract: Through considerable effort and intuition, several recent works have reverse-engineered nontrivial behaviors of transformer models. This paper systematizes the mechanistic interpretability process they followed. First, researchers choose a metric and dataset that elicit the desired model behavior. Then, they apply activation patching to find which abstract neural network units are involved in the behavior. By varying the dataset, metric, and units under investigation, researchers can understand the functionality of each component. We automate one of the process' steps: to identify the circuit that implements the specified behavior in the model's computational graph. We propose several algorithms and reproduce previous interpretability results to validate them. For example, the ACDC algorithm rediscovered 5/5 of the component types in a circuit in GPT-2 Small that computes the Greater-Than operation. ACDC selected 68 of the 32,000 edges in GPT-2 Small, all of which were manually found by previous work. Our code is available at https://github.com/ArthurConmy/Automatic-Circuit-Discovery.

papers.title: Group Equivariance Meets Mechanistic Interpretability: Equivariant Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can group symmetries be incorporated into sparse autoencoders for mechanistic interpretability, and does this lead to more useful features in downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces adaptively equivariant sparse autoencoders that incorporate group symmetries, which learn features leading to superior probing performance compared to regular SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Adding domain-specific properties like group equivariance to sparse autoencoders can significantly increase their utility in domains beyond language, despite being early results.
papers.key_findings:
A single matrix M can explain more than 98% of the variance in how neural network activations transform under input transformations by a discrete cyclic group.
Equivariant SAEs learn more informative directions in activation space, leading to increased performance on group-structured probing tasks.
Equivariant SAEs lag behind regular SAEs in the reconstruction/sparsity frontier.
papers.limitation: Results are limited to a synthetic task, relatively small models, and a small discrete group.
future_direction: Can M be learned as effectively in larger models such as frontier foundation models?
Can the optimization of M be improved by better utilizing the group structure, e.g., by constraining the optimization to M^|G| = I?
Does the two-layer encoder qualitatively alter what kind of features are discovered, and how can the features best be labeled incorporating the knowledge of how they transform with M?
Can the reconstruction performance of the equivariant SAE be improved to match that of regular SAEs?
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have proven useful in disentangling the opaque activations of neural networks, primarily large language models, into sets of interpretable features. However, adapting them to domains beyond language, such as scientific data with group symmetries, introduces challenges that can hinder their effectiveness. We show that incorporating such group symmetries into the SAEs yields features more useful in downstream tasks. More specifically, we train autoencoders on synthetic images and find that a single matrix can explain how their activations transform as the images are rotated. Building on this, we develop adaptively equivariant SAEs that can adapt to the base model's level of equivariance. These adaptive SAEs discover features that lead to superior probing performance compared to regular SAEs, demonstrating the value of incorporating symmetries in mechanistic interpretability tools.

papers.title: The Physics of Data and Tasks: Theories of Locality and Compositionality in Deep Learning
papers.research_question: What is the latent structure of learnable data, and how do neural networks encode and exploit it to achieve generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The thesis develops a theoretical framework showing that locality and compositionality in data and tasks enable deep networks to overcome the curse of dimensionality, and demonstrates that diffusion models learn hierarchical grammars and that task arithmetic in pre-trained models is enabled by weight disentanglement.
papers.conclusion: This thesis proposes that deep learning is effective because it operates on a cascade of compositional structures, from local features to hierarchical representations and modular organization of knowledge in weight space.
papers.key_findings:
Locality in CNNs allows them to overcome the curse of dimensionality by adapting to the spatial scale of the target function.
Diffusion models exhibit a phase transition during generation, revealing the hierarchical compositionality of natural data.
The sample complexity for learning hierarchical grammars scales polynomially with dimension, explaining how diffusion models avoid the curse of dimensionality.
Weight disentanglement in pre-trained models enables task arithmetic and model editing.
Hierarchical learning requires feature learning, not just kernel methods.
papers.limitation: The Random Hierarchy Model, while rich, is still a simplification of natural data.
future_direction: Extending the theory to other generative models (e.g., autoregressive models)
Understanding the emergence of weight disentanglement during pre-training
Scaling laws for hierarchical learning
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success, yet our understanding of how they learn remains limited. These models can learn high-dimensional tasks, which is generally statistically intractable due to the curse of dimensionality. This apparent paradox suggests that learnable data must have an underlying latent structure. What is the nature of this structure? How do neural networks encode and exploit it, and how does it quantitatively impact performance - for instance, how does generalization improve with the number of training examples? This thesis addresses these questions by studying the roles of locality and compositionality in data, tasks, and deep learning representations. We begin by analyzing convolutional neural networks in the limit of infinite width, where the learning dynamics simplifies and becomes analytically tractable. Using tools from statistical physics and learning theory, we characterize their generalization abilities and show that they can overcome the curse of dimensionality if the target function is local by adapting to its spatial scale. We then turn to more complex structures in which features are composed hierarchically, with elements at larger scales built from sub-features at smaller ones. We model such data using simple probabilistic context-free grammars - tree-like graphical models used to describe data such as language and images. Within this framework, we study how diffusion-based generative models compose new data by assembling features learned from examples. This theory of composition predicts a phase transition in the generative process, which we confirm empirically in both image and language modalities, providing support for the compositional structure of natural data. We further demonstrate that the sample complexity for learning these grammars scales polynomially with data dimension, providing a mechanism by which diffusion models avoid the curse of dimensionality by learning to hierarchically compose new data. These results offer a theoretical grounding for how generative models learn to generalize, and ultimately, become creative. Finally, we shift our analysis from the structure of data in the input space to the structure of tasks in the model's parameter space. Here, we investigate a novel form of compositionality, where tasks and skills themselves can be composed. In particular, we empirically demonstrate that distinct directions in the weight space of large pre-trained models are associated with localized, semantic task-specific areas in function space, and how this modular structure enables task arithmetic and model editing at scale.

papers.title: Cross-Model Semantics in Representation Learning
papers.research_question: How do structural constraints affect the compatibility of internal representations across different architectures? To what extent are learned representations tied to specific architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper formalizes representational alignment across architectures and demonstrates that structural regularities induce more stable representational geometry, improving interoperability of learned features.
papers.conclusion: PGNN integrates structural priors to enhance learning efficiency and generalization, and structural constraints can improve representational transferability across models.
papers.key_findings:
PGNN exhibits faster convergence and slightly higher test accuracy compared to baseline MLP.
Ablation shows that removing structural projection in PGNN leads to lower performance, confirming its utility.
PGNN shows similar robustness to initialization noise as MLP, with slight advantages under mild noise.
Representational alignment metrics show that structured representations can be partially aligned across architectures.
The framework enables measurement of alignment using CKA, subspace overlap, and transfer accuracy.
papers.limitation: Extrapolation to more complex datasets like CIFAR-10 did not show a major advantage for PGNN.
future_direction: Adapting and scaling PGNN to broader domains and more complex data distributions.
papers.abstract: The internal representations learned by deep networks are often sensitive to architecture-specific choices, raising questions about the stability, alignment, and transferability of learned structure across models. In this paper, we investigate how structural constraints--such as linear shaping operators and corrective paths--affect the compatibility of internal representations across different architectures. Building on the insights from prior studies on structured transformations and convergence, we develop a framework for measuring and analyzing representational alignment across networks with distinct but related architectural priors. Through a combination of theoretical insights, empirical probes, and controlled transfer experiments, we demonstrate that structural regularities induce representational geometry that is more stable under architectural variation. This suggests that certain forms of inductive bias not only support generalization within a model, but also improve the interoperability of learned features across models. We conclude with a discussion on the implications of representational transferability for model distillation, modular learning, and the principled design of robust learning systems.

papers.title: High-dimensional manifold of solutions in neural networks: insights from statistical physics
papers.core_contribution: The paper reviews the statistical mechanics approach to neural networks, focusing on the perceptron model, and explains how the geometry of the solution space (manifold of solutions) changes with the size of the training set.
papers.key_findings:
The SAT/UNSAT transition separates a satisfiable phase where solutions exist from an unsatisfiable phase where the solution set is empty.
In the binary perceptron, typical solutions are isolated, but there exist subdominant, wide flat minima that are algorithmically accessible.
The local entropy transition marks a change in the geometry of solution regions and is connected to the onset of algorithmic hardness in binary models.
In the spherical negative perceptron, the solution space is star-shaped, with a kernel region from which any other solution can be reached via a zero-error geodesic path.
Linear mode connectivity between solutions can be characterized analytically, revealing the structure of the solution manifold.
papers.abstract: In these pedagogic notes I review the statistical mechanics approach to neural networks, focusing on the paradigmatic example of the perceptron architecture with binary an continuous weights, in the classification setting. I will review the Gardner's approach based on replica method and the derivation of the SAT/UNSAT transition in the storage setting. Then, I discuss some recent works that unveiled how the zero training error configurations are geometrically arranged, and how this arrangement changes as the size of the training set increases. I also illustrate how different regions of solution space can be explored analytically and how the landscape in the vicinity of a solution can be characterized. I give evidence how, in binary weight models, algorithmic hardness is a consequence of the disappearance of a clustered region of solutions that extends to very large distances. Finally, I demonstrate how the study of linear mode connectivity between solutions can give insights into the average shape of the solution manifold.

papers.title: Dictionary Learning Improves Patch-Free Circuit Discovery in Mechanistic Interpretability: A Case Study on Othello-GPT
papers.research_question: How do we recognize circuits connecting the enormous amount of dictionary features extracted via sparse dictionary learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a patch-free circuit discovery framework that uses dictionary learning to decompose model activations into monosemantic features and then traces contributions between these features to identify interpretable circuits, avoiding out-of-distribution issues and improving asymptotic complexity compared to patching-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary learning enables patch-free circuit discovery, providing a macroscopic view of the model's internal information flow and turning microscopic understanding into a more comprehensive one.
papers.key_findings:
The framework successfully identifies interpretable dictionary features in Othello-GPT, such as current move position, board state, empty cells, and legal move features.
It discovers a local OV circuit that computes board state by combining information from previous moves via specific attention heads.
The QK circuit's attention patterns (e.g., attending to opponent's moves) are implemented through resonance between low-level dictionary feature pairs representing move colors.
Early MLP layers identify flipped pieces by performing an 'and' operation on features representing consecutive moves on a line, with attention heads introducing color information.
papers.limitation:
The dictionary training may have used too small sparsity coefficients, leading to near-perfect reconstruction and about 75% dead neurons in each dictionary.
The QK decomposition only interprets individual attention scores and fails to account for the relative strength introduced by the Softmax normalization across the sequence.
Approximate Direct Contribution (ADC) for MLPs is an approximation that treats part of the activation function input as constant.
Circuit analysis is based on specific inputs and does not claim universal understanding of the model; discovering general motifs is left for future work.
future_direction: Discovering general motifs in Transformers is a central problem left for future work.
Alleviating the dictionary training problem of dead neurons to achieve deeper understanding.
Extending the method to language models, which have sparser features and a more complex world compared to the Othello task.
papers.abstract: Sparse dictionary learning has been a rapidly growing technique in mechanistic interpretability to attack superposition and extract more human-understandable features from model activations. We ask a further question based on the extracted more monosemantic features: How do we recognize circuits connecting the enormous amount of dictionary features? We propose a circuit discovery framework alternative to activation patching. Our framework suffers less from out-of-distribution and proves to be more efficient in terms of asymptotic complexity. The basic unit in our framework is dictionary features decomposed from all modules writing to the residual stream, including embedding, attention output and MLP output. Starting from any logit, dictionary feature or attention score, we manage to trace down to lower-level dictionary features of all tokens and compute their contribution to these more interpretable and local model behaviors. We dig in a small transformer trained on a synthetic task named Othello and find a number of human-understandable fine-grained circuits inside of it.

papers.title: Same Task, Different Circuits: Disentangling Modality-Specific Mechanisms in VLMs
papers.research_question: Why do Vision-Language models (VLMs) perform worse on visual tasks compared to analogous textual tasks?
papers.core_contribution: VLMs use largely disjoint circuits for visual and textual tasks, but the functional difference lies in data processing; patching visual token embeddings from later layers to earlier layers (back-patching) reduces the performance gap without training.
papers.conclusion: The performance gap in VLMs arises from disjoint circuits for different modalities, and back-patching provides a training-free method to reduce it by aligning visual representations earlier.
papers.key_findings:
Vision and language circuits are structurally disjoint but implement similar functionalities for query and generation.
The performance gap stems from differences in processing modality-specific data tokens.
Visual token representations become aligned with textual counterparts only in later layers.
Back-patching visual token embeddings from later to earlier layers improves visual task accuracy, closing about a third of the performance gap on average.
The intervention is effective across multiple models and tasks.
papers.limitation:
Focused on single-image question-answering tasks with single-token completions.
Current open models struggle with complex visual reasoning, limiting analysis.
Circuit analysis methods are limited to single-token completions.
Back-patching closes only 32% of the performance gap; causes for the remaining gap are unclear.
Analysis is limited to adapter-based VLMs; may not apply to other fusion approaches.
future_direction: Explore multi-image scenarios, different prompt orders, and more complex visual reasoning tasks.
Investigate varied computational resources per token, especially for visual inputs.
Extend analysis to VLMs with different fusion approaches.
papers.abstract: Vision-Language models (VLMs) show impressive abilities to answer questions on visual inputs (e.g., counting objects in an image), yet demonstrate higher accuracies when performing an analogous task on text (e.g., counting words in a text). We investigate this accuracy gap by identifying and comparing the \textit{circuits} - the task-specific computational sub-graphs - in different modalities. We show that while circuits are largely disjoint between modalities, they implement relatively similar functionalities: the differences lie primarily in processing modality-specific data positions (an image or a text sequence). Zooming in on the image data representations, we observe they become aligned with the higher-performing analogous textual representations only towards later layers, too late in processing to effectively influence subsequent positions. To overcome this, we patch the representations of visual data tokens from later layers back into earlier layers. In experiments with multiple tasks and models, this simple intervention closes a third of the performance gap between the modalities, on average. Our analysis sheds light on the multi-modal performance gap in VLMs and suggests a training-free approach for reducing it.

papers.title: Toy Models of Superposition
papers.research_question: Why do neurons sometimes align with interpretable features and sometimes not, and how can neural networks represent more features than they have dimensions (superposition)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that superposition—where neural networks store more sparse features than dimensions—is a real phenomenon, explains polysemanticity, and reveals a phase change and geometric structure in feature representations.
papers.conclusion: Superposition occurs in neural networks, allowing them to represent more features than dimensions, which has important implications for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Superposition is a real, observed phenomenon in neural networks.
Both monosemantic and polysemantic neurons can form.
At least some kinds of computation can be performed in superposition.
Whether features are stored in superposition is governed by a phase change.
Superposition organizes features into geometric structures such as digons, triangles, pentagons, and tetrahedrons.
papers.limitation:
The toy models are simple and it is unclear what to generalize to real networks.
The ReLU hidden layer toy model has a weakness where the model circumvents the activation function if possible.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often pack many unrelated concepts into a single neuron - a puzzling phenomenon known as 'polysemanticity' which makes interpretability much more challenging. This paper provides a toy model where polysemanticity can be fully understood, arising as a result of models storing additional sparse features in "superposition." We demonstrate the existence of a phase change, a surprising connection to the geometry of uniform polytopes, and evidence of a link to adversarial examples. We also discuss potential implications for mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: APP: Accelerated Path Patching with Task-Specific Pruning
papers.research_question: Can pruning be used for circuit discovery, and how can we accelerate path patching by reducing the search space?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Accelerated Path Patching (APP), a hybrid method that uses Contrastive-FLAP pruning to reduce the search space for circuit discovery, achieving significant speedups while recovering minimal circuits with performance comparable to standard path patching.
papers.conclusion: APP provides a scalable preprocessing step for circuit discovery, making mechanistic interpretability more efficient and practical for large models.
papers.key_findings:
Pruning alone cannot recover minimal circuits; circuits found by pruning are larger than those found by path patching.
Contrastive-FLAP, a novel pruning method, better preserves task-specific attention heads compared to vanilla FLAP.
APP reduces the search space for circuit discovery by an average of 56%, leading to speedups of 59.63%-93.27% compared to standard path patching.
Circuits discovered by APP have substantial overlap and similar performance to those found by standard path patching.
APP enables circuit discovery to scale to larger models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B) by reducing computational costs.
papers.limitation:
Hyperparameter search is limited by computational cost, especially for large models.
Trade-off between circuit size and performance requires researcher discretion.
APP focuses on attention heads and does not include MLP components, which may be important for some tasks.
The true positive rate of hybrid FLAP caps the ability to recover all heads in the circuit.
future_direction: Extending APP to other circuit discovery algorithms like ACDC.
Incorporating MLP components into the automated path patching method.
Studying whether circuits discovered in GPT-2 small translate to larger models.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery is a key step in many mechanistic interpretability pipelines. Current methods, such as Path Patching, are computationally expensive and have limited in-depth circuit analysis for smaller models. In this study, we propose Accelerated Path Patching (APP), a hybrid approach leveraging our novel contrastive attention head pruning method to drastically reduce the search space of circuit discovery methods. Our Contrastive-FLAP pruning algorithm uses techniques from causal mediation analysis to assign higher pruning scores to task-specific attention heads, leading to higher performing sparse models compared to traditional pruning techniques. Although Contrastive-FLAP is successful at preserving task-specific heads that existing pruning algorithms remove at low sparsity ratios, the circuits found by Contrastive-FLAP alone are too large to satisfy the minimality constraint required in circuit analysis. APP first applies Contrastive-FLAP to reduce the search space on required for circuit discovery algorithms by, on average, 56\%. Next, APP, applies traditional Path Patching on the remaining attention heads, leading to a speed up of 59.63\%-93.27\% compared to Path Patching applied to the dense model. Despite the substantial computational saving that APP provides, circuits obtained from APP exhibit substantial overlap and similar performance to previously established Path Patching circuits

papers.title: A circuit for predicting hierarchical structure in-context in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether induction heads in LLMs can support in-context learning of complex repetitive patterns with hierarchical dependencies, and how these induction heads themselves learn in-context.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs use adaptive induction heads that learn to attend to correct successor tokens in hierarchical contexts, supported by context matching heads that encode latent contexts, providing a mechanistic account of in-context learning for repetitive patterns.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that LLMs use adaptive induction heads and context matching heads to learn hierarchical dependencies in-context, offering a mechanistic account of in-context learning for repetitive patterns.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads in LLMs can learn to attend to correct successor tokens in-context for sequences with hierarchical dependencies.
Adaptive induction heads are located in later layers, while static induction heads are in earlier layers.
Ablating induction heads severely reduces prediction accuracy, showing their causal role in in-context learning.
Context matching heads encode latent chunk identities and are causally involved in enabling induction heads to learn.
The proposed circuit of context matching heads feeding into induction heads explains hierarchical in-context learning, including in natural language ambiguous cases.
papers.limitation:
The study has not explored other types of in-context learning, such as abstract reasoning tasks like the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC).
All learning analyzed happens non-verbally, without explicit verbal reasoning or deliberation.
future_direction: Study induction head behavior in abstract reasoning tasks like the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC).
Study induction head behavior in settings with verbal reasoning and deliberation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at in-context learning, the ability to use information provided as context to improve prediction of future tokens. Induction heads have been argued to play a crucial role for in-context learning in Transformer Language Models. These attention heads make a token attend to successors of past occurrences of the same token in the input. This basic mechanism supports LLMs' ability to copy and predict repeating patterns. However, it is unclear if this same mechanism can support in-context learning of more complex repetitive patterns with hierarchical structure. Natural language is teeming with such cases: The article "the" in English usually prefaces multiple nouns in a text. When predicting which token succeeds a particular instance of "the", we need to integrate further contextual cues from the text to predict the correct noun. If induction heads naively attend to all past instances of successor tokens of "the" in a context-independent manner, they cannot support this level of contextual information integration. In this study, we design a synthetic in-context learning task, where tokens are repeated with hierarchical dependencies. Here, attending uniformly to all successor tokens is not sufficient to accurately predict future tokens. Evaluating a range of LLMs on these token sequences and natural language analogues, we find adaptive induction heads that support prediction by learning what to attend to in-context. Next, we investigate how induction heads themselves learn in-context. We find evidence that learning is supported by attention heads that uncover a set of latent contexts, determining the different token transition relationships. Overall, we not only show that LLMs have induction heads that learn, but offer a complete mechanistic account of how LLMs learn to predict higher-order repetitive patterns in-context.

papers.title: Do Llamas understand the periodic table?
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models (LLMs) represent the periodic table of elements, and what is the geometric structure of their hidden states?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs internally develop structured geometric representations (a 3D spiral) of the periodic table in their hidden states, with knowledge encoded as continuous manifolds in middle layers that sharpen into categorical distinctions in deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: LLMs represent symbolic scientific knowledge as coherent, geometry-aware manifolds that reflect the natural order of the physical world, which can inform interpretability and trust in LLMs for scientific applications.
papers.key_findings:
A 3D spiral structure in LLM hidden states aligns with the conceptual organization of the periodic table.
Middle layers encode continuous, overlapping attribute subspaces, while deeper layers sharpen decision boundaries and integrate linguistic context.
Linguistic structure increasingly shapes factual representations in later layers.
Strong linear associations between related attributes in middle layers enable indirect recall.
Regression probing shows continuous numerical features are effectively represented in intermediate layers, while classification probing shows later layers are better for fine-grained categorical decisions.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to chemical elements in the periodic table; future studies could expand to other chemical structures and properties.
The hypothesis-driven validation of geometric structures may oversimplify LLMs' non-linear interactions.
future_direction: Expand to other chemical structures and properties.
Further investigation into how LLMs represent and reason about scientific knowledge.
papers.abstract: We observe a 3D spiral structure in the hidden states of LLMs that aligns with the conceptual structure of the periodic table.

papers.title: Interpreting Neural Networks through the Polytope Lens
papers.research_question: What are the fundamental primitives of neural network representations, and can polytopes serve as a better unit of description than neurons or directions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the polytope lens, a perspective that accounts for nonlinearities in neural networks, and demonstrates that polytopes can identify monosemantic regions and that polytope boundaries correspond to semantic boundaries.
papers.conclusion: The polytope lens provides a more accurate description of neural networks by incorporating nonlinearities, but further work is needed to develop it into a practical tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Polysemantic directions overlap with multiple monosemantic polytope regions.
Polytope boundaries reflect semantic boundaries, with denser boundaries between different classes than within the same class.
Polytopes partially define when feature-directions are on- and off-distribution, with dense boundaries near the origin but class changes also occur in low-density regions.
Clustering activations or spline codes yields monosemantic clusters in both image classifiers and language models.
The polytope lens provides a more complete description of neural networks by incorporating nonlinearities, but it is not yet clear how to use it for decomposable descriptions.
papers.limitation: The polytope lens sacrifices globally valid feature directions for locally valid ones, making descriptions more complex and less decomposable.
future_direction: Develop the polytope lens into a practical tool for mechanistic interpretability.
Build more robust and scalable methods based on the polytope lens.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to explain what a neural network has learned at a nuts-and-bolts level. What are the fundamental primitives of neural network representations? Previous mechanistic descriptions have used individual neurons or their linear combinations to understand the representations a network has learned. But there are clues that neurons and their linear combinations are not the correct fundamental units of description: directions cannot describe how neural networks use nonlinearities to structure their representations. Moreover, many instances of individual neurons and their combinations are polysemantic (i.e. they have multiple unrelated meanings). Polysemanticity makes interpreting the network in terms of neurons or directions challenging since we can no longer assign a specific feature to a neural unit. In order to find a basic unit of description that does not suffer from these problems, we zoom in beyond just directions to study the way that piecewise linear activation functions (such as ReLU) partition the activation space into numerous discrete polytopes. We call this perspective the polytope lens. The polytope lens makes concrete predictions about the behavior of neural networks, which we evaluate through experiments on both convolutional image classifiers and language models. Specifically, we show that polytopes can be used to identify monosemantic regions of activation space (while directions are not in general monosemantic) and that the density of polytope boundaries reflect semantic boundaries. We also outline a vision for what mechanistic interpretability might look like through the polytope lens.

papers.title: The Representational Status of Deep Learning Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether deep learning models are representational in a relational sense and to what extent they are semantically decomposable.
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that deep learning models are representational in a relational sense, but they are minimally semantically decomposable (holistic) models, and there is no evidence that they encode locally decomposable representations of their targets.
papers.conclusion: Deep learning models are best conceived as holistic representational models, and interpreting them as locally decomposable is epistemically risky.
papers.key_findings:
Deep learning models are representational in a relational sense (they have real targets).
Deep learning models are not locally semantically decomposable; their representational capacity is global/holistic.
Opacity blocks a full assessment of the representational status of deep learning models.
Attempts to interpret deep learning models as locally decomposable are underdetermined and unfalsifiable.
The degree of idealization of a deep learning model cannot be evaluated due to opacity.
future_direction: Future analysis on situating deep learning models in the wider class of holistic models.
Exploring how deep learning models can be leveraged for scientific discovery without relying on local decomposability.
papers.abstract: This paper aims to clarify the representational status of Deep Learning Models (DLMs). While commonly referred to as 'representations', what this entails is ambiguous due to a conflation of functional and relational conceptions of representation. This paper argues that while DLMs represent their targets in a relational sense, in general, we have no good reason to believe that DLMs encode locally semantically decomposable representations of their targets. That is, the representational capacity these models have is largely global, rather than decomposable into stable, local subrepresentations. This result has immediate implications for explainable AI (XAI) and directs attention toward exploring the global relational nature of deep learning representations and their relationship both to models more generally to understand their potential role in future scientific inquiry.

papers.title: Rethinking LLM-as-a-Judge: Representation-as-a-Judge with Small Language Models via Semantic Capacity Asymmetry
papers.research_question: Can small language models serve as efficient evaluators by leveraging internal representations, even when their generation is poor?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Semantic Capacity Asymmetry Hypothesis and introduces INSPECTOR, a probing-based framework that extracts evaluation signals from small model representations, enabling efficient and accurate reference-free evaluation.
papers.conclusion: Small LMs retain strong evaluative signals in their internal representations, and the Representation-as-a-Judge paradigm via INSPECTOR offers a scalable and interpretable solution for evaluation and data curation.
papers.key_findings:
Small LMs encode rich evaluative signals in their hidden states despite weak generation.
Probing internal representations with INSPECTOR outperforms prompt-based evaluation with small LMs and closely approximates large LLM judges.
The Semantic Capacity Asymmetry Hypothesis is supported: evaluation requires less semantic capacity than generation.
Probing classifiers can serve as reliable data filters for supervised fine-tuning, leading to performance gains.
Larger LLMs do not necessarily provide stronger evaluation signals than smaller ones.
papers.limitation:
Multiclass prediction performance of probing classifiers is modest (50-60%) compared to binary classification.
Out-of-distribution generalization for multiclass probing is limited, with F1 scores dropping significantly.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used as reference-free evaluators via prompting, but this "LLM-as-a-Judge" paradigm is costly, opaque, and sensitive to prompt design. In this work, we investigate whether smaller models can serve as efficient evaluators by leveraging internal representations instead of surface generation. We uncover a consistent empirical pattern: small LMs, despite with weak generative ability, encode rich evaluative signals in their hidden states. This motivates us to propose the Semantic Capacity Asymmetry Hypothesis: evaluation requires significantly less semantic capacity than generation and can be grounded in intermediate representations, suggesting that evaluation does not necessarily need to rely on large-scale generative models but can instead leverage latent features from smaller ones. Our findings motivate a paradigm shift from LLM-as-a-Judge to Representation-as-a-Judge, a decoding-free evaluation strategy that probes internal model structure rather than relying on prompted output. We instantiate this paradigm through INSPECTOR, a probing-based framework that predicts aspect-level evaluation scores from small model representations. Experiments on reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, GPQA) show that INSPECTOR substantially outperforms prompting-based small LMs and closely approximates full LLM judges, while offering a more efficient, reliable, and interpretable alternative for scalable evaluation.

papers.title: Persona Features Control Emergent Misalignment
papers.research_question: When, why, and how does fine-tuning language models on narrow incorrect datasets lead to broad, undesirable misalignment (emergent misalignment), and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Emergent misalignment occurs across diverse fine-tuning and reinforcement learning settings and is mediated by 'misaligned persona' features in activation space, which can be used to detect, steer, and mitigate the behavior.
papers.conclusion: Emergent misalignment is a robust phenomenon that can arise from various training procedures, and interpretability methods like model-diffing with sparse autoencoders can reveal its mechanistic basis and enable detection and mitigation strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Emergent misalignment occurs from supervised fine-tuning on narrow incorrect advice in diverse domains and from reinforcement learning that rewards incorrect responses.
A 'toxic persona' feature (and other related features) identified via sparse autoencoder model-diffing causally controls emergent misalignment and can be used to steer model behavior.
Fine-tuning an emergently misaligned model on a few hundred benign samples efficiently re-aligns the model.
The activation level of the 'toxic persona' feature can discriminate between aligned and misaligned models, serving as a potential early-warning signal.
Emergent misalignment generally increases with model size for models capable of coherent responses.
papers.limitation: Fine-tuning on natural human-generated data produces high incoherence and correlated misalignment, which may be a different effect from the emergent misalignment observed with synthetic data.
future_direction: Further work to understand training dynamics, especially the effects of off-policy fine-tuning on human data.
papers.abstract: Understanding how language models generalize behaviors from their training to a broader deployment distribution is an important problem in AI safety. Betley et al. discovered that fine-tuning GPT-4o on intentionally insecure code causes "emergent misalignment," where models give stereotypically malicious responses to unrelated prompts. We extend this work, demonstrating emergent misalignment across diverse conditions, including reinforcement learning on reasoning models, fine-tuning on various synthetic datasets, and in models without safety training. To investigate the mechanisms behind this generalized misalignment, we apply a "model diffing" approach using sparse autoencoders to compare internal model representations before and after fine-tuning. This approach reveals several "misaligned persona" features in activation space, including a toxic persona feature which most strongly controls emergent misalignment and can be used to predict whether a model will exhibit such behavior. Additionally, we investigate mitigation strategies, discovering that fine-tuning an emergently misaligned model on just a few hundred benign samples efficiently restores alignment.

papers.title: Position-aware Automatic Circuit Discovery
papers.research_question: How can we incorporate positional information into automatic circuit discovery for language models to address limitations of position-agnostic methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces position-aware circuit discovery (PEAP) and dataset schemas to enable fully automated discovery of position-sensitive circuits, achieving better faithfulness than position-agnostic methods.
papers.conclusion: Position-aware circuit discovery and schemas improve circuit faithfulness and enable automated analysis of variable-length inputs, providing a more precise foundation for mechanistic explanations.
papers.key_findings:
Position-aware circuits are smaller and more faithful than position-agnostic circuits.
Automatically generated schemas (with or without saliency masks) yield circuits comparable to those from human-designed schemas.
The proposed method handles variable-length inputs via schemas, enabling circuit discovery in more naturalistic settings.
papers.limitation:
Schemas assume sequential order of spans, which may not hold for all datasets.
The schema generation and application pipeline may not always produce valid schemas for all examples.
future_direction: Relax the sequential order assumption in schemas to support greater variation across examples.
Investigate the components in the circuit for the Winobias task to understand the balance between task-relevant and bias-inducing factors.

papers.title: Uncovering Emergent Physics Representations Learned In-Context by Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models implicitly learn physics during in-context learning, and do recognizable physical quantities emerge as distinct features in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that large language models can learn to forecast physical dynamics via in-context learning, and that energy-related features emerge in their residual stream activations, which are causally important for accurate predictions.
papers.conclusion: The results demonstrate that LLMs can internalize physical concepts like energy during in-context learning, suggesting transformer architectures can internalize abstract reasoning priors similar to human abstraction.
papers.key_findings:
Prediction accuracy for physical dynamics forecasting improves with longer context length.
Sparse activations from sparse autoencoders (SAEs) applied to residual streams correlate with energy quantities (total, kinetic, potential).
The correlation between sparse activations and energy is context-dependent and increases with longer contexts, especially for chaotic systems.
Intervention experiments ablating energy-correlated sparse activations degrade prediction accuracy, indicating their functional role.
Energy-related features are most prominently captured in the middle layers of the transformer.
papers.limitation: The study uses raw trajectory values as the sole input modality without external instructions or prompting strategies, leaving open whether chain-of-thought or structured prompts would strengthen correlations.
future_direction: Explore physics concepts beyond classical mechanics.
Investigate more human-aligned tasks such as answering conceptual questions from physics exams.
Leverage physics-informed tasks to understand internal mechanisms of large-scale models and advance LLM-based agents for physically realistic environments.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive in-context learning (ICL) abilities, enabling them to solve wide range of tasks via textual prompts alone. As these capabilities advance, the range of applicable domains continues to expand significantly. However, identifying the precise mechanisms or internal structures within LLMs that allow successful ICL across diverse, distinct classes of tasks remains elusive. Physics-based tasks offer a promising testbed for probing this challenge. Unlike synthetic sequences such as basic arithmetic or symbolic equations, physical systems provide experimentally controllable, real-world data based on structured dynamics grounded in fundamental principles. This makes them particularly suitable for studying the emergent reasoning behaviors of LLMs in a realistic yet tractable setting. Here, we mechanistically investigate the ICL ability of LLMs, especially focusing on their ability to reason about physics. Using a dynamics forecasting task in physical systems as a proxy, we evaluate whether LLMs can learn physics in context. We first show that the performance of dynamics forecasting in context improves with longer input contexts. To uncover how such capability emerges in LLMs, we analyze the model's residual stream activations using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). Our experiments reveal that the features captured by SAEs correlate with key physical variables, such as energy. These findings demonstrate that meaningful physical concepts are encoded within LLMs during in-context learning. In sum, our work provides a novel case study that broadens our understanding of how LLMs learn in context.

papers.title: CoT Vectors: Transferring and Probing the Reasoning Mechanisms of LLMs
papers.research_question: Can we transfer the essence of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning into LLMs in a compact, reusable, and efficient way? Also, how can CoT Vectors be used to probe the underlying mechanisms of reasoning in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CoT Vectors, compact representations that encode task-general, multi-step reasoning knowledge, and proposes Learnable CoT Vectors optimized via a teacher-student framework for more stable and robust guidance.
papers.conclusion: CoT Vectors extend the task vector paradigm to multi-step reasoning, and Learnable CoT Vectors provide stronger and more stable gains, while also serving as a valuable probe into the mechanisms and organization of reasoning in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Extracted CoT Vectors show a U-shaped performance curve across layers, revealing a three-stage reasoning process (perception, reasoning, expression) in LLMs.
Learnable CoT Vectors outperform extracted vectors and are more stable across layers.
CoT Vectors achieve performance comparable to parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like LoRA while requiring orders of magnitude fewer trainable parameters.
The effectiveness of CoT Vectors varies with latent space structure, information density, acquisition mechanisms, and pre-training differences.
CoT Vectors can be used as a probe to analyze the functional organization of reasoning in LLMs.
papers.limitation:
Performance variability in intermediate layers highlights structural limitations, suggesting that task-level vectors may not fully capture intra-task diversity.
CoT Vectors can sometimes interfere with correct reasoning paths and lead to incorrect answers, as shown in case studies.
future_direction: Explore finer-grained or adaptive vectorization strategies to improve robustness and generalization.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has emerged as a powerful approach to enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing implementations, such as in-context learning and fine-tuning, remain costly and inefficient. To improve CoT reasoning at a lower cost, and inspired by the task vector paradigm, we introduce CoT Vectors, compact representations that encode task-general, multi-step reasoning knowledge. Through experiments with Extracted CoT Vectors, we observe pronounced layer-wise instability, manifesting as a U-shaped performance curve that reflects a systematic three-stage reasoning process in LLMs. To address this limitation, we propose Learnable CoT Vectors, optimized under a teacher-student framework to provide more stable and robust guidance. Extensive evaluations across diverse benchmarks and models demonstrate that CoT Vectors not only outperform existing baselines but also achieve performance comparable to parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, while requiring fewer trainable parameters. Moreover, by treating CoT Vectors as a probe, we uncover how their effectiveness varies due to latent space structure, information density, acquisition mechanisms, and pre-training differences, offering new insights into the functional organization of multi-step reasoning in LLMs. The source code will be released.

papers.title: A Toy Model of Universality: Reverse Engineering How Networks Learn Group Operations
papers.research_question: The paper investigates the universality hypothesis: whether different models learn similar features and circuits when trained on similar tasks, by studying how small neural networks learn to implement group composition.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the group composition via representations (GCR) algorithm and shows that neural networks consistently learn this algorithm when trained on group composition tasks, providing evidence for weak universality (underlying principles exist) but against strong universality (specific circuits vary).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that while there is an underlying algorithm (GCR) that networks learn for group composition, the specific features and circuits are arbitrary, supporting weak universality but not strong universality.
papers.key_findings:
Networks learn the GCR algorithm for group composition, which uses representation theory to compute compositions.
The specific representations (circuits) learned vary across different runs and hyperparameters, indicating that while the algorithm is universal, the implementation is not.
The order in which representations are learned is arbitrary and not consistent across runs.
The network's logits can be approximated as a sum of characters from a sparse set of representations.
Ablations confirm that the identified components are causally important for the task.
papers.limitation: The algorithm does not perfectly explain all logits due to limitations of the architecture (e.g., ReLU activations imperfectly implement matrix multiplication).
future_direction: Extending to other group theoretic tasks such as conjugacy, group actions, and automata.
Studying semigroups (which lack representation theory).
Investigating inductive biases of networks more broadly.
papers.abstract: Universality is a key hypothesis in mechanistic interpretability -- that different models learn similar features and circuits when trained on similar tasks. In this work, we study the universality hypothesis by examining how small neural networks learn to implement group composition. We present a novel algorithm by which neural networks may implement composition for any finite group via mathematical representation theory. We then show that networks consistently learn this algorithm by reverse engineering model logits and weights, and confirm our understanding using ablations. By studying networks of differing architectures trained on various groups, we find mixed evidence for universality: using our algorithm, we can completely characterize the family of circuits and features that networks learn on this task, but for a given network the precise circuits learned -- as well as the order they develop -- are arbitrary.

papers.title: Is This Just Fantasy? Language Model Representations Reflect Human Judgments of Event Plausibility
papers.research_question: How do language models internally represent modal categories (probable, improbable, impossible, inconceivable)? How do these representations develop, do they reflect human categorization behavior, and what interpretable features do they correspond to?
papers.core_contribution: Language models form linear representations (modal difference vectors) that distinguish between modal categories (probable, improbable, impossible, inconceivable). These vectors are more diagnostic than output probabilities, emerge in an intuitive order during training, and reflect fine-grained human categorization behavior and interpretable features like event likelihood and imageability.
papers.conclusion: Language models learn internal representations of modal categories that go beyond output probabilities. These representations develop in an intuitive order and capture nuanced aspects of human categorization, offering a novel way to study world models in LMs and potentially human cognition.
papers.key_findings:
Modal difference vectors within LM hidden states reliably classify sentences by modal category, outperforming classification based on sentence probability.
Modal difference vectors develop in a consistent order: inconceivable vs. others emerges first, followed by probable vs. impossible, then probable vs. improbable, and finally improbable vs. impossible.
Projections of sentences onto modal difference vectors create a feature space that accurately models human participants' graded categorization judgments.
Projections along the impossible-inconceivable vector correlate selectively with human ratings of imageability and the presence of physical objects/places.
Preliminary steering experiments show that adding modal difference vectors to the residual stream during generation can influence the modal category of the generated text.
future_direction: Using modal difference vectors to test the intuitive theories about the world that LMs encode from text.
Using modal difference vectors to generate hypotheses about human representations of modal categories, such as the role of imagination in distinguishing impossible from inconceivable events.
papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) are used for a diverse range of tasks, from question answering to writing fantastical stories. In order to reliably accomplish these tasks, LMs must be able to discern the modal category of a sentence (i.e., whether it describes something that is possible, impossible, completely nonsensical, etc.). However, recent studies have called into question the ability of LMs to categorize sentences according to modality (Michaelov et al., 2025; Kauf et al., 2023). In this work, we identify linear representations that discriminate between modal categories within a variety of LMs, or modal difference vectors. Analysis of modal difference vectors reveals that LMs have access to more reliable modal categorization judgments than previously reported. Furthermore, we find that modal difference vectors emerge in a consistent order as models become more competent (i.e., through training steps, layers, and parameter count). Notably, we find that modal difference vectors identified within LM activations can be used to model fine-grained human categorization behavior. This potentially provides a novel view into how human participants distinguish between modal categories, which we explore by correlating projections along modal difference vectors with human participants' ratings of interpretable features. In summary, we derive new insights into LM modal categorization using techniques from mechanistic interpretability, with the potential to inform our understanding of modal categorization in humans.

papers.title: Questioning Representational Optimism in Deep Learning: The Fractured Entangled Representation Hypothesis
papers.research_question: Does better performance necessarily imply better internal representations? This paper challenges the view of representational optimism by comparing the internal representations of networks trained via open-ended search versus conventional stochastic gradient descent (SGD).
papers.core_contribution: The paper challenges representational optimism by introducing the Fractured Entangled Representation (FER) hypothesis, demonstrating that networks trained with conventional SGD can develop disorganized internal representations (FER) even when output performance is good, whereas networks from open-ended search can achieve more organized Unified Factored Representations (UFR).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that Fractured Entangled Representation (FER) is a potential issue in conventional deep learning, raising questions about the adaptability of models trained via SGD, and that understanding and mitigating FER could be critical for the future of representation learning.
papers.key_findings:
Networks trained with conventional SGD to produce a target image exhibit Fractured Entangled Representations (FER), where information for unitary concepts is split into disconnected, redundant pieces that become entangled.
Networks evolved through the open-ended Picbreeder process for the same output image exhibit Unified Factored Representations (UFR), where concepts are represented in a single, modular, and reusable manner.
Weight sweeps reveal that UFR networks allow for meaningful, human-recognizable variations (e.g., changing symmetry, stem angle) while respecting regularities, whereas FER networks produce deleterious, entangled changes that break regularities.
The path (curriculum) taken during learning influences the final representation; open-ended search discovers fundamental regularities (like symmetry) early, which are then elaborated upon, while conventional SGD takes a direct, greedy path.
The paper speculates that FER in large models may underlie challenges in generalization, creativity, and continual learning, and that the order in which concepts are learned is fundamental to the quality of the internal representation.
papers.limitation:
The study is conducted on a minimal, toy task (generating a single image) using CPPNs/MLPs, which is far simpler than large-scale models like LLMs.
The implications of FER for large models are speculative and based on analogy and limited examples of LLM behavior.
future_direction: Investigate FER in large models like LLMs and explore ways to mitigate it.
Study the impact of curricula and the ordering of concepts during training on the development of FER/UFR.
Explore alternative training algorithms and objectives (e.g., open-ended, novelty-seeking) that might lead to better internal representations.
papers.abstract: Much of the excitement in modern AI is driven by the observation that scaling up existing systems leads to better performance. But does better performance necessarily imply better internal representations? While the representational optimist assumes it must, this position paper challenges that view. We compare neural networks evolved through an open-ended search process to networks trained via conventional stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on the simple task of generating a single image. This minimal setup offers a unique advantage: each hidden neuron's full functional behavior can be easily visualized as an image, thus revealing how the network's output behavior is internally constructed neuron by neuron. The result is striking: while both networks produce the same output behavior, their internal representations differ dramatically. The SGD-trained networks exhibit a form of disorganization that we term fractured entangled representation (FER). Interestingly, the evolved networks largely lack FER, even approaching a unified factored representation (UFR). In large models, FER may be degrading core model capacities like generalization, creativity, and (continual) learning. Therefore, understanding and mitigating FER could be critical to the future of representation learning.

papers.title: Machine Learning Topological Invariants with Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Can neural networks learn topological invariants from local inputs and generalize to predict winding numbers for Hamiltonians with larger winding numbers not seen during training?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that neural networks can successfully learn global topological invariants from local Hamiltonian inputs, generalize to predict winding numbers beyond the training range, and internally learn the discrete winding number formula.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can learn global and nonlinear topological features from local inputs and exhibit strong generalization power, opening possibilities for using machine learning to study topological physics.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks can predict topological winding numbers with nearly 100% accuracy, even for Hamiltonians with larger winding numbers not included in the training data.
Convolutional networks outperform fully-connected networks due to their inherent translation symmetry, which matches the symmetry of the winding number problem.
By analyzing the internal function of the convolutional network, the authors confirm it learns the discrete version of the winding number formula.
Regularization techniques like L2 regularization can harm generalization when training data are noise-free, but become beneficial when noise is present.
If training data are restricted to a specific model (e.g., the SSH model), the network may learn shortcuts based on local symmetries and fail to generalize to more general Hamiltonians.
papers.limitation:
Regularization techniques can be detrimental to generalization when the training data are noise-free.
If the training data are restricted to a specific model with additional symmetries, the neural network may learn shortcuts and fail to generalize to more general cases.
future_direction: Generalize the results to topological models in higher dimensions and other symmetry classes.
Apply the trained network to analyze data from quantum simulators.
papers.abstract: In this Letter we supervisedly train neural networks to distinguish different topological phases in the context of topological band insulators. After training with Hamiltonians of one-dimensional insulators with chiral symmetry, the neural network can predict their topological winding numbers with nearly 100% accuracy, even for Hamiltonians with larger winding numbers that are not included in the training data.
